title: Attachment Styles
description: The biological and psychological framework dictating how people bond, seek proximity, and handle intimacy.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: Attachment styles are subconscious survival strategies developed in childhood that dictate how an adult behaves in relationships. They determine how much proximity a person tolerates, how they handle conflict, and what they do when they feel threatened.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Anxious: Needs constant reassurance, double texts, feels rejected easily.
Avoidant: Withdraws when things get too intimate, values independence over connection.
Fearful-Avoidant: Desires closeness but panics when it happens, creating push-pull dynamics.
Secure: Comfortable with intimacy, handles conflict without panic, gives partners space without anxiety.

sections.title: Why It Happens
content: Inconsistent caregiving in childhood trains the brain to anxiously constantly seek connection.
Emotionally unavailable caregiving trains the brain to self-soothe and avoid relying on others.
A biological drive to ensure safety through either hyper-vigilance or complete self-reliance.
Past relational trauma that reinforced negative beliefs about trust and safety.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Anxious: Stalking social media, seeking excessive reassurance, adopting the partner's interests.
Avoidant: Finding fatal flaws in partners, scheduling heavy workloads to avoid dates, intellectualizing feelings.
Secure: Direct communication of needs, respecting boundaries, assuming positive intent.

sections.title: Healthy Version
sections.content: Secure Attachment: The ability to deeply emotionally invest in a partner while maintaining a separate sense of self. It involves effectively self-soothing during conflict and repairing ruptures directly without emotional withdrawal or desperate clinging.

sections.title: Unhealthy Version
sections.content: Insecure Attachment Loop (The Anxious-Avoidant Trap): An anxious person chases connection, causing the avoidant person to feel suffocated and withdraw. The withdrawal triggers severe abandonment fears in the anxious person, causing them to chase harder, further repelling the avoidant. It is a highly toxic, self-sustaining system.

sections.title: Real-Life Scenarios
content: Dating: An avoidant partner goes silent for three days after a highly intimate weekend because their nervous system needs to 'reset'.
Marriage: An anxious spouse starts a fight about doing the dishes, because the negative attention feels safer than feeling ignored.
Friendship: A secure friend calmly says, 'I need some space this week, but let's catch up Sunday', leaving the other person feeling totally safe.

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: Sudden, unexplained withdrawal after a period of intense closeness.
Extreme jealousy or panic when a partner does something independently.
A relationship history consisting entirely of explosive, on-and-off dynamics.
A constant feeling that you must 'earn' someone's consistent presence.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: Mistake: Assuming an avoidant partner 'just needs more love' to open up, or that an anxious partner 'just needs to calm down'. Reality: These are nervous system responses to perceived threats. More love triggers an avoidant's fear of engulfment. Logic does not soothe an anxious person's fear of abandonment.

sections.title: Protection Strategies
content: Identify your own baseline style to recognize when you are operating out of fear.
Stop interpreting an avoidant's need for space as a referendum on your worth.
Stop interpreting an anxious person's bid for connection as a desire to control you.
If you are insecurely attached, actively date secure partners. Their consistency will slowly rewire your nervous system.

sections.title: Outcome Patterns
content: Anxious + Anxious: Often burns out quickly due to mutual codependency and high volatility.
Avoidant + Avoidant: Often drifts apart naturally into roommates as neither initiates deep emotional connection.
Anxious + Avoidant: The most common and most painful trap, resulting in a lifelong cycle of chasing and running.
Secure + Anyone: The secure partner usually stabilizes the insecure partner, or calmly leaves if the dynamic is too toxic.

sections.title: Reality Check
sections.content: Attachment styles exist on a spectrum and can change depending on your environment, current stress levels, and the attachment style of the person you are currently with. You are not permanently 'broken' if you lean insecure.
